The main reason I didn't opt to use `directories` is that the macOS and Windows directories are deep and rarely known by users. As much as I'd like to follow a standard, the majority of apps end up dropping their dotfiles in the home directory, which makes it the easy choice for others.

I'd be open to changing it, but I feel like the added complexity of it being different on each system will increase the barrier to use Starship. Telling the user to create `~/.config/starship.toml` is easy and consistent.

I've seen this go both ways before: the Kitty developer is very zealous about strictly maintaining platform-specific conventions, with the result that there's a mega-issue on kitty with users asking for the exact opposite of this :P

I don't think it'd necessarily be a bad idea to support the platform convention. We'd then need to add support for e.g. duplicate config files, conflicting configs, and so on.
I'm of course willing to defer to the community, but I think it'd be preferable to the system convention but allow for `starship --config ~/.config/starship.toml`.

One big advantage I see is not having to think about it. It's in XDG standard directories, done. There's also an env variable that anyone can use if they think the standard location is in a hard to find place.

In summary, I don't think being different justifies, even if the argument for it is good.

Edit: @matchai I just saw your statement about other apps putting their config in the home directory as well. Maybe we won't ever agree which ones are majority (really depends on which ones you use), but I'd be happier to see one more app following the standard. There's that XKCD.

As a Windows user, nowadays I've actually come to expect CLI tools to have their config in HOME. Even Microsoft is using `~/.dotnet` and `~/.nuget`.

Also consider that `AppData` isn't supposed to be a place for users to dig around in, so it's fine to use it to store data generated by your application but if a user is supposed to edit it, it should not be there. Since `starship.toml` is very much supposed to be edited by the user and there is no settings UI, it definitely should not be in `AppData`.

If anything, the Windows-native convention here would be the Documents folder, which is what PowerShell is doing for its $PROFILE (`~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1`). But let's not go there ;)

Sorry to comment on such an old issue, but I created [a crate called Etcetera](https://docs.rs/etcetera) that, in my opinion, addresses `directories`’s problem of using _too_ platform-specific locations. It does this by allowing the library consumer to pick and choose different ‘strategies’ (ways of picking config locations) as they wish, without having to re-specify the name and author of the application.

Let’s say that Starship chooses to use the Unix-ish convention of `~/.app-name/config-file` on all platforms. Here’s how you would use it with Etcetera:

```rust
use etcetera::app_strategy::{AppStrategy, AppStrategyArgs, Unix};

let args = AppStrategyArgs {
    top_level_domain: "rs".to_string(),
    author: "Starship Contributors".to_string(),
    app_name: "Starship".to_string(),
};

let strategy = Unix::new(args)?;

let config_dir = strategy.config_dir(); // ~/.starship/
let config_file = strategy.in_config_dir("config.toml"); // ~/.starship/config.toml
```

If instead you decide to use XDG instead of the Unix convention, all that’s needed is to change one line (well, two if you count the `use`):

```rust
use etcetera::app_strategy::{AppStrategy, AppStrategyArgs, Xdg}; // changed!

let args = AppStrategyArgs {
    top_level_domain: "rs".to_string(),
    author: "Starship Contributors".to_string(),
    app_name: "Starship".to_string(),
};

let strategy = Xdg::new(args)?; // changed!

let config_dir = strategy.config_dir(); // ~/.config/starship/
let config_file = strategy.in_config_dir("config.toml"); // ~/.config/starship/config.toml
```

Note that this actually follows the [XDG spec](https://specifications.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/basedir-spec-latest.html):

- It uses the value of the `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` environment variable if it exists
- It doesn’t respect `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and falls back to `~/.config` if it is a relative path

There are also strategies available for [Apple](https://docs.rs/etcetera/0.3/etcetera/app_strategy/struct.Apple.html) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/etcetera/0.3/etcetera/app_strategy/struct.Windows.html).

> Note that this actually follows the XDG spec:
It uses the value of the XDG_CONFIG_HOME environment variable if it exists
It doesn’t respect $XDG_CONFIG_HOME and falls back to ~/.config if it is a relative path
There are also strategies available for Apple and Windows.

I also agree with this setting method.
`~/.config/starship.toml` is very confusing for users as it is different from many other apps.
If follow XDG Base Directory Specification, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/starship/<filename>.toml` will be the correct path.

I remember in [this issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustup/issues/247) where some Windows users disagreed with XDG, since putting a `.` before a file or folder’s name doesn’t actually hide it. This means they end up with a `.config` folder for that one application that uses XDG. Etcetera has a [Windows](https://docs.rs/etcetera/0.3/etcetera/app_strategy/struct.Windows.html) strategy available that picks the appropriate location in `~/AppData`.

On Windows, my home directory currently has the following dot files.

```
.config/
.dotnet/
.m2/
.nuget/
.ssh/
.angular-config.json
.gitconfig
.npmrc
.yarnrc
```

On the other hand, I can't recall a time that I've ever accessed or updated a dot file in `%AppData%`.

I guess you could use the [Unix](https://docs.rs/etcetera/0.3/etcetera/app_strategy/struct.Unix.html) strategy on Windows and [Xdg](https://docs.rs/etcetera/0.3/etcetera/app_strategy/struct.Xdg.html) everywhere else. The irony of using the Unix strategy only on Windows is not lost on me 😄
Any plans on implementing this?

Not for the time being. The existing precedent of tools using `~/.config`, low barrier of entry for beginners, and the consistency in cross-platform documentation support our decision to use the home directory.

If you'd prefer to use platform-specific configuration, you can override Starship's config location with the following:
```sh
export STARSHIP_CONFIG=$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/starship.toml
```

All modern modern cli tools such as fish, tig, neovim, and git support xdg, so I think xdg is easier for beginners to understand.
https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/XDG_Base_Directory

The same applies to the cache directory as well. I have my `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` set to `~/Library/Caches` instead of `~/.cache` for not having to tell my backup tools an extra directory to exclude beyond the macOS standard, but Starship keeps on recreating an (always empty??) `~/.cache/starship` dir.

For config however, I'm strongly opposing `~/Library`. This is afaik mostly used by GUI program's configs, which are not meant to be edited by hand. Every CLI tool, or to say it another way, every config I edit as a text file, lives either in `~/.config` or directly in home on Mac the same way as on most other Unix-derived platforms.

Lastly, above it is suggested that `~/.config/starship/config.toml` is better than having it in .config directly. ~~This is neither backed by the standard (it just doesn't mention whether to use folders inside .config or not)~~(Edit: I'm wrong. I like `~/.config/starship.toml` more nevertheless), nor does it make sense to me. My opinion: If a tool needs more than one file for configuration (like Neovim or Fish), a subdir is the way to go, but I don't need a directory for containing one single file.

I think the point is obeying the specification of XDG or not instead of how many files one directory contains.

windows user here - I expected starship to use XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Was surprised that it didn't.

I carefully move all files from my C drive (which is small) to my larger drive, which is where my XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set. The other linux-y tools I use do this fine.

>Not for the time being. The existing precedent of tools using ~/.config

As far as I am aware, the only reason apps migrated from `.appname/` to `.config/appname/` is the XDG spec.
I agree with all the comments regarding simply using the HOME folder in MacOS - it is a secondary de-facto standard for CLI apps and for manually edited text files, reserving `$HOME/Library/Application Support` for GUI applications that are primarily configured through their own GUI. I am relatively unfamiliar with the situation on Windows, though it's been mentioned (https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/896#issuecomment-604088042) %APPDATA% is not a place for the user to dig around in.

My personal reasons for preferring a `starship` subdirectory in `.config` is on the one hand simply having the consistency of knowing everything there is a subdirectory. Second to that, there is an [issue](https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/3039) regarding preset imports. Currently, one can't simply import a preset or some settings, instead they must be prepended to `.config/starship.toml`. I imagine that regarding that issue having a `starship/` subdirectory is a boon.

If this were ever decided to be implemented, a backwards compatible way is to attempt to use `$HOME/.config/starship.toml` - or the appropiate legacy location in the corresponding platform - by default and rely on `XDG_CONFIG_HOME/starship/` and `.config/starship/` as a fallback.

 This is implemented in #5282 - included the check for `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`.

TLDR: there's a backwards compatible PR (5282) that respects the user's choice whether to use the current value or XDG environment variable location, in that order. 

Does that have any drawbacks? The platform specific location issue is addressed by just using .config across platforms, and I do not think documenting users to use `.config/starship/config.toml` is an issue either.

One thing to point out is that starship doesn't manage to follow any existing standards either.
Older unix-like programs would use paths like `~/.<app>rc` or `~/.<app>/<configfile>`.
Modern unix-like programs use `~/.config/<app>/<configfile>`. This is exactly the path introduced and recommended by the XDG BaseDir philosophy.

The `~/.config/starship.toml` path that Starship uses now doesn't seem to meet either of these standards. It looks like a mix of the two, but it's not a universal standard. Something like this may happens when an old style unix-like tool later decides to support XDG BaseDir, but in order to maintain backward compatibility, finally decides to put the original single configuration file `~/.<app>rc` directly into the XDG `~/.config/` directory instead of `~/.config/<app>/<configfile>`.
So Starship‘s approach seems like it's not being thought through.

Exactly. Just follow the spec on linux and allow users to opt out. Out of all the tools that I'm storing config files for, `starship` is the only one with this approach.

[This open PR](https://github.com/starship/starship/pull/6690)  seems promising and sane. Going forward lean towards XDG, but have a reasonable fallback in cases where existing config might exist.

There's a reason us stubborn XDG zealots keep asking for this. The intersection of starship being incredible and also an outlier in this admittedly minor but itchy regard.

Yeah, I just hit this as well. I expected it would be `~/.config/starship/config.toml` or `~/.config/starship/starship.toml`. I'm trying to automate config file deployment... One of these things is not like the others...

I also just encountered this peculiarity when updating the developer environments for our org.

I just want to add that if the config file path ever changes this would be a breaking change.

As a Linux user who likes to be able to quickly restore all my settings on a new system, I created symbolic links of pretty much all my config files pointing to files in a git repository. This way, I can very easily and regularly commit all my settings changes and push to remote (and of course clone the repo and apply all symbolic links to quickly restore my settings).

It's fine to make breaking changes, but I'd expect to see a major version increment if Semantic versioning is respected. 
So if one day my settings suddenly stopped working, seeing the major version increase would immediately point me to check the changelog and understand what happened.

> It's fine to make breaking changes, but I'd expect to see a major version increment if Semantic versioning is respected.

If such a breaking change were to be implemented, just have the default prompt put a note about the path change and/or look for a few common places users had their old config. The default prompt would be invoked for a "missing" configuration file. I think Starship has great workaround potential that will minimize the pain for users using non-standard-but-original-starhsip-behavior.
I think the plan is to do a major version increment when this matures https://github.com/starship/starship-poc
